title: [Pinoy Criminology] Killing of judges threatens the rule of law
summary: A country that cannot protect its judges cannot promise its people a fair hearing, a just decision, or the rule of law

blocks.text: Another judge has fallen to assassins, and another court has been left to mourn. Judge Joseph Wee Sit, presiding over Branch 2 of the Regional Trial Court in Isabela City, Basilan, was shot dead in Zamboanga City on November 12. He was a young judge, only a little over a year into service on the bench, with his life and public service still opening before him.

This should outrage not only the legal profession, but the entire Filipino community. The killing is horrifying on its own, but it also carries a danger beyond one family’s grief. Every bullet fired at a judge is a threat to the institution that must decide disputes by law.

Whether this killing was intended to intimidate the judiciary remains for investigators to establish. But we cannot pretend an attack on a judge is merely a private crime, detached from public office. Judges sometimes confront politically charged, contested cases, where their decisions threaten interests powerful enough to answer law with force.

That possibility makes the killing all the more urgent to investigate, without prematurely declaring who ordered it or why. A murder can terrorize a court before its motive becomes known, because judges understand the warning implicit in violence.

The judiciary is supposed to be impartial and independent. Judges swear to decide cases on their merits, on the facts presented, and the law that governs them. They must be able to rule without fear or favor, even when their decisions anger the powerful or disappoint the public. When judges know that their lives, limbs, and careers are on the line, safety can begin to shape judgment. Then decisions are made not on merit, but on power; that is rule by men, not rule of law.

I have written about judgments arriving after 21 years, people trapped in judicial limbo, and detention prolonged by vacancies and delay. Those problems may look different from the murder of a judge, but they expose the same fragility. A court cannot guard liberty when it lacks time, personnel, and resources to hear cases fairly and promptly. Nor can the public trust justice when the law’s guardians are left vulnerable, unsupported, or pressured by political power. The judge should be the immediate guardian of liberty, and accountability separates justice from mere force.

That protection begins before a judge enters the courtroom. It begins with the appointment process, where judicial posts must never become prizes in partisan warfare. If lawyers must beg political patrons for judicial posts, obligations and loyalty tests can precede their first ruling. That is an unfair burden to place on young, idealistic lawyers, then send them to decide cases affecting the lives and fortunes of powerful people. Appointments must rest on merit alone, measured through integrity, ability, experience, and the courage to apply law equally.

The Judicial and Bar Council must be strengthened in its work of recruiting, selecting, and recommending judges and justices. Malacañang, as the final appointing authority, must respect the council’s merit-based recommendations and choose the most qualified candidates. That principle has too often remained aspirational, invoked in speeches but weakened by political calculation. An appointment system based on merit gives judges legitimacy and weakens patrons’ leverage over the bench. It also assures the public that judicial office is earned through qualification and service, rather than political loyalty.

We must also strengthen the judiciary after appointment. Congress and the presidency must provide more judges, court staff, functioning offices, and dependable operational budgets. Judges cannot deliver justice effectively when they lack the personnel, equipment, and basic resources to do their work. Courts should not have to depend on mayors, governors, or legislators for support that belongs to the national government. Local officials must respect independence, while the national government ensures judges never depend on local favor.

Protection must be real, sustained, and visible, especially for judges serving in places where cases carry exceptional risks. That means assessing threats, protecting court personnel, and coordinating security without letting security arrangements compromise judicial independence.

The investigation must establish who killed Judge Wee Sit, identify any instigators, and determine whether the attack was connected to his work. The Supreme Court has mobilized its judicial marshals to work with law enforcement, a necessary step toward accountability. The state must also stand with his family and every judge who returns to court despite danger.

Otherwise, judges will be reduced from instruments of law to instruments of the powerful. Disgruntled politicians, criminals, and businessmen will learn that terror can clear a judge from their path. Young lawyers attracted to public service will see that idealism can cost them their lives, while the state offers little protection.

That is how fear enters the courtroom, and how justice quietly yields to those who can threaten it. A country that cannot protect its judges cannot promise its people a fair hearing, a just decision, or the rule of law. – Rappler.com
Raymund E. Narag, PhD, is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at the School of Justice and Public Safety, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale.
